title: Calibrating a syringe pump by gravimetry
content:
Delivered flow depends on two things: how far the drive head travels (pump mechanics) and the syringe bore you program. Weighing the water measures only their product, so calibrate them in order — do it backwards and a mechanics error hides inside a wrong "effective diameter": Pump mechanics first (Step 1) — so the drive head moves the true distance. Syringe diameter second (Steps 2–5) — the balance then corrects the bore alone. The gravimetric part needs only an analytical balance — water weighs ~1 g/mL, so 1 mg ≈ 1 µL: 
Q_real = mass / (ρ_water · time)
D_real = D₀ · √(Q_real / Q_set)
If the balance reads more than programmed → the syringe is wider than you told the pump → increase the diameter. The calculator calibrate.py does the math; you just type the numbers. Equipment Analytical balance, 1 mg (0.001 g); 0.1 mg is even better. Dial indicator or digital caliper (0.01 mm) — to measure drive-head travel (Step 1). Syringe under test, filled with bubble-free distilled water. Parafilm + a small receiving tube (e.g. Eppendorf). Tweezers/tongs for handling calibration weights (skin oil weighs enough to matter). The syringe pump. Step 0 — Calibrate the balance (once) Place it on a stable, level table (centre the bubble with the feet); no drafts, sun or vibration. Warm it up for ≥ 1 hour powered on. Empty pan, reading 0.0. Enter external calibration (on CGOLDENWALL/JoanLab HZ-type balances: Set → menu → e-cal; it requests a standard weight, e.g. cal-200 = 200 g). Place the exact standard weight with tongs, wait, remove when prompted → returns to 0.0. Verify: place a known weight (e.g. 100 g) and check it reads correctly. Step 1 — Calibrate the pump mechanics (plunger travel) First check the mechanics on their own: does the drive head move the distance you command? This is the displacement method of EURAMET CG-27 §4.3.3 — lab version uses a laser interferometer; workshop version uses a dial indicator (command a known move, measure the real travel, correct the firmware's steps/mm — exactly how a 3D-printer axis is calibrated). Mount a dial indicator (or caliper) against the drive head / carriage and zero it. Run the pump empty — this test is purely mechanical. Command a long move L_set (e.g. 20.00 mm) so the ±0.01 mm reading error is negligible. Read the actual travel L_real. Correct the firmware constant: steps_per_mm_corr = steps_per_mm × (L_real / L_set). Repeat over the full stroke (0→20, 20→40 mm …) to catch lead-screw non-uniformity. No dial indicator? A caliper — or even a ruler — measures the same travel; just use a longer move (e.g. 50–100 mm) so the coarser reading stays a small fraction of the distance. Step 2 — Prepare the gravimetric run Fill the syringe, purge all air (a single bubble ruins a run). Mount it in the pump. Program the nominal diameter D₀ (caliper the inner bore, or use the syringe spec) and the target flow Q_set. Let the pump drip into any waste tube until the flow is steady — we use 5 min; the first minutes clear residual bubbles and let the mechanics settle. Step 3 — Collect the output, weighed (timed collection) Prepare the collection tube first: close the empty Eppendorf, seal the top with parafilm, pierce a small hole with the sharp tip of scissors (just big enough for the capillary — keeps evaporation low), and stand it on a small, very light base (we cut one from packing foam — negligible mass, keeps the round-bottom tube upright on the pan). Weigh it in this final state (tube + parafilm + hole + foam base) → m_empty, or tare to zero. Then collect, without stopping the flow: with the flow already steady, move the capillary from the waste tube into the collection tube through the parafilm hole, and start the stopwatch at that instant. Collect for an exactly timed interval t. Move the capillary out, press the parafilm closed over the hole, and weigh immediately → m_full. Δm = m_full − m_empty.

1 — Caliper the bore to get the nominal diameter D₀
2 — Seal the tube top with parafilm
3 — Pierce a small hole with a scissor tip
4 — Insert the capillary through the hole
Aim for Δm ≥ 100 mg (e.g. 10 min at 1000 µL/h ≈ 167 mg → <1 % uncertainty at 1 mg). Step 4 — Compute the corrected diameter ➡️ Open the web calculator — type the weighed values, get the corrected diameter (no install). 
python3 calibrate.py --d0 8.94 --qset 1000 --mass 170.5 --minutes 10 --temp 20
#   flow real (balance): 1024.8 uL/h  (+2.5 %)
#   CORRECTED DIAMETER : 9.05 mm   <- enter this on the pump
Enter D_real on the pump. Repeat one point to confirm Q_real ≈ Q_set. Step 5 — Verify linearity Repeat at 2–3 flows (e.g. 500 / 1000 / 2000 µL/h) with the corrected diameter. If they all give the same D_real, the calibration is solid and flow-independent. Background (optional) Delivered flow = drive-head speed × syringe cross-section. Gravimetry sees only the product, so a wrong lead-screw pitch looks exactly like a wrong bore — that's why Step 1 (travel) comes before Step 4 (bore). Many open-hardware pumps skip the split and fold both into one "effective diameter" per pump (Wijnen & Pearce, 2014): accurate flow, but you no longer know which part was off. Mechanism cycle. A lead-screw pump's flow has a slow ripple at the screw's turn period (EURAMET CG-27). Collect over ≥ 2 full turns to average it out — it's expected, not a bubble. Practical tips (what ruins a run) Evaporation: at 1000 µL/h an open tube loses ~1 mg/min — always parafilm, and weigh immediately after capping. Weights with tongs, never fingers. Exclude the first ~5 min of each run (stabilization + bubble clearing). Record water temperature; the tool adjusts density (20 °C → 0.99821 g/mL). ±2 °C is negligible (<0.1 %). Bubbles: purge before, and if the output suddenly spikes/dips erratically, there is air in the line — stop and purge. Optional: cross-check with a flow sensor (higher precision) The balance fixes the diameter. If you also have an in-line flow sensor, the same runs let you check — and calibrate — the sensor against the balance (ground truth), then use the sensor as a continuous flow reference without weighing every time. calibrate.py reports the sensor factor if you pass --sensor-ulh <reading>. For the flow-sensor hardware, firmware and high-rate acquisition, see the Rio controller: ➡️ wenzel-lab/rio-controller (pressure/flow module). EURAMET is the European Association of National Metrology Institutes — the body that defines SI-traceable measurement in Europe. IPQ (Instituto Português da Qualidade) is Portugal's national metrology institute; Elsa Batista (IPQ) leads both the guide and the displacement-method papers above.
